newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon sees Aug start on oil pipeline from Chad.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon sees Aug start on oil pipeline from Chad.

text.p: The much-delayed construction of an oil pipeline between land-locked Chad and the Cameroonian port town of Kribi could begin in August, Cameroon's acting energy minister said on Tuesday.

"The final agreement between the governments of Chad and Cameroon for the transportation of Chadian oil has been reached and construction work could begin next month," Jean-Baptiste Bokam said in a debate on his ministry's budget.

Exxon Corp announced an agreement last November with the government of Chad, under which a consortium led by its subsidiary, Esso Exploration and Production Chad Inc, would begin the first commercial production of oil in the country.
It estimated it would need $3 billion for developing the reserves in the Doba Basin, 350 miles south of Chad's capital, N'Djamena, plus infrastructure costs including the pipeline.
The partners are looking for funding from international financial institutions.
Cameroon minister Bokam repeated the $3 billion figure on Tuesday, adding that $2 billion would be needed for the pipeline alone.

He said that Exxon would have a 34.6 percent stake in the project, the same as Royal Dutch/Shell. France's Elf Aquitaine would have 17.3 percent, the government of Chad five percent and Cameroon National Hyrdrocarbon Company 8.5 percent.
Exxon said in November that the project area contained about 900 million barrels of recoverable reserves. Further prospecting is going on in the west of Chad.
The pipeline that will take the oil to the coast to be exported will be about 1,050 km (650 miles) long, with 880 km of that in Cameroon.
Both Exxon and the government of Chad, an impoverished former French colony, have said that commercial production would begin before 2000.
Small-scale oil production in Chad during the 1970s came to a halt because of civil war and persistent security problems.

The original framework agreement for this latest project was signed in January 1995. In May this year, Chadian President Idriss Deby said part of the blame for the delay in starting the project lay with French environmentalists and with locals concerned they would not benefit. -- Abidjan newsroom +225 21 90 90
